To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“The correlation between two strength modes of a population can be estimated from a single proof-loading test, using only the proportion of the population that breaks in each mode and the mean and standard deviation of the weaker mode, provided the population is bivariate normal.”

(a) the correlation between two strength modes can be estimated by using only proof loading, (b) the correlation estimate is asymptotically normally distributed, (c) the asymptotic variance can be estimated from the proof-load data, (d) the asymptotic distribution of the correlation estimate can be used to construct confidence intervals, and (e) the confidence interval is a function of the individual means, variances, and proof-load level.
In summary, our research is concerned with
estimating the bivariate normal parameters from proof-load data.
the estimation of the correlation parameter of two variables that can only be measured destructivly.
the estimation of the correlation between two strength modes when only destructive testing is possible.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the assumption of no damage to survivors is reasonable, but not completely true.
the assumption is reasonable, but not proven.

, although there is some evidence to support the assumption that proof-loaded survivors are not damaged, further experimental work is needed before the assumption can be considered to be generally applicable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the procedures proposed in this paper provide reasonable estimates of the correlation between two strength modes when the proof load is sufficiently large.
we have shown that it is possible to obtain reasonable estimates of all five bivariate parameters from a single destructive testing procedure.
the proposed methods can be used to estimate all five bivariate parameters of the normal distribution, provided the assumption of no damage to the survivors is valid.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, if a proof-load is chosen to be large enough to break only about 5% of the population, one can estimate the correlation between the strength modes of the survivors with reasonable accuracy.
, in situations where the correlation between strength modes is important, the cost of a proof-loading experiment is well worth the expense.
the estimation of correlations is feasible using proof-loading.
